title: The Coverage Problem Nobody Wants to Talk About
summary: Same 412 accounts. Same 5-contact cap. Same director-plus brief. LeadGenius still delivered 36% more contacts and nearly 2x the director-level coverage.
body_markdown:
Clay vs. LeadGenius: The Coverage Gap That Holds at the Same Cap | LeadGenius KEY FINDINGS


- At the same 5-contact cap, **LeadGenius found 36% more contacts** than Clay across the same 412 target accounts (496 vs. 364).
- The cap only changed the count on **1 in 8 accounts** . On the other 87% of the list, LeadGenius's own output was already at or under 5.
- Only **34% of Clay's contacts** actually met the director-level-plus brief we gave it. LeadGenius hit **56%** .
- Layer coverage and seniority together, and Clay's *usable* output for this GTM motion isn't 364 contacts. It's closer to **121** .
- The gap was widest at the largest, best-documented accounts, exactly where it should be smallest, raising the question of what happens further down market.


Clay closed a $115 million Series D this week at a $7.1 billion valuation, more than double where it stood thirteen months ago. Wellington Management led the round. Sequoia, a16z, and CapitalG came back for another lap. By the numbers investors care about, Clay is now one of the fastest-appreciating companies in the go-to-market software category, and the company says it's on pace to roughly double its revenue again next year.


None of that tells you what happens when you actually point Clay at a list of target accounts and ask it to do the job it's being valued for. So we did that instead. We took 412 companies, mid-market and larger SaaS businesses that sell into the SMB segment, and asked two data providers, Clay and LeadGenius, to do the same job: find contacts in a handful of go-to-market roles, director level and above. GTM engineers. RevOps. Marketing ops.


Clay was capped at five contacts per company by design. LeadGenius wasn't, so before comparing anything, we capped it too, at the same five, and checked one more thing the raw counts never show: whether the contacts each tool actually returned matched the seniority we asked for in the first place.


Both cuts moved the story. Neither one changed the conclusion. A company can raise at $7.1 billion and still miss on the basic, unglamorous task of finding the right person at the right company. Those two facts aren't in tension. They're just measuring different things, and only one of them is measured by asking the tool to actually do the work.


## The gap holds at the same cap


Cap both tools at five contacts per company and Clay found 364. LeadGenius found 496. That's the honest, apples-to-apples number, still 36% more than Clay, from the same list, under the same constraint.


Clay total contacts


364


LeadGenius, same 5/company cap


496


It's worth being precise about how much the cap actually mattered. Matching LeadGenius to Clay's five-contact ceiling only changed the count on 53 of the 412 accounts, the 12.9% of the list where LeadGenius's own search found more than five people. For the other 87% of the list, LeadGenius's real output was already at or under five, meaning the cap only ever applied to one account in eight. Level that one-in-eight difference completely, and LeadGenius still wins on total volume by more than a third.


## The part where the tool just doesn't answer


Volume is one story. Coverage is the one that actually determines whether a rep has a territory to work. Sixty-eight percent of the time, 282 accounts out of 412, Clay returned nothing. Not "we found one contact who didn't quite match." Nothing. LeadGenius struck out less often: 245 accounts, or 60%.


A zero doesn't feel like a data problem to the rep who inherits it. It feels like a dead territory, a market that "doesn't have anyone in RevOps," which is very rarely true and very often just means the tool didn't look hard enough. The account doesn't get worked. Nobody escalates it, because there's nothing to escalate. There's just an absence, and absences don't generate tickets.


219 accounts (53%) came back empty from both tools, a shared blind spot neither vendor's graph reaches. Outside that dead zone, the two tools don't fail the same way: LeadGenius found unique coverage on 63 accounts Clay couldn't touch at all, while Clay's unique wins numbered 26. Head to head, at the same cap, LeadGenius delivered more contacts than Clay on 29.6% of all 412 accounts; Clay came out ahead on 12.9%.


> When LeadGenius and Clay disagreed on an account, LeadGenius found more people 2.3 times more often than Clay did, even after Clay's structural advantage on volume was removed.


---


## The titles weren't the titles we asked for


Here's the finding that didn't show up in the first pass, because we hadn't gone looking for it: we told Clay, explicitly, to search for director-level-plus titles. Directors, VPs, heads of function, C-suite. That was the brief. It's not what came back.


Of the 357 individual contacts in Clay's output, *only 121, about one in three, actually cleared the director-plus bar we asked for* . The rest were managers, senior managers, individual contributors, and a large "other" bucket of titles that don't map to seniority at all. LeadGenius, searching the same accounts for the same roles, returned 997 contacts of which 563, 56%, cleared that same bar. Not perfect. Notably better.


Clay: share meeting director-plus bar


34%


LeadGenius: share meeting director-plus bar


56%


What makes this worse than a simple accuracy miss is what it does to the volume number. Clay's 364 contacts already looked thin against LeadGenius's 496. But 364 was never really the usable number. It was the number before you filtered for the thing you actually asked the tool to find. Once you filter for seniority, Clay's usable output for this GTM motion isn't 364. It's closer to 121. That's not a coverage gap anymore. That's a coverage gap on top of a precision problem, and the two compound rather than offset.


What "director-level plus" actually looked like in Clay's output


- **Marketing Operations Associate** , tagged "Other"
- **Revenue Operations Specialist** , tagged "Staff"
- **Revenue Operations Data Analyst** , tagged "Staff"
- **Marketing Operations Manager II** , tagged "Manager"
- **Regional Online Marketing Operations** , tagged "Other," no seniority signal in the title at all
- **Marketing Operations & Automation Manager** , tagged "Manager"


None of these are bad hires or irrelevant contacts in some general sense. A Marketing Operations Manager is a perfectly reasonable person to know at a company. They're just not who we asked for, and if a rep is working a list assuming it's been pre-filtered to decision-maker level, the actual seniority mix underneath the count is the difference between a productive call and a wasted one.

## Why this matters more, not less, as you move down market


Here's where I want to be honest about the limits of what this dataset can tell you, because the honesty is more persuasive than the alternative. This list, 412 companies, skews toward larger, well-documented organizations. These are the accounts where a data provider should have the easiest time, the most public org charts, the most LinkedIn presence to work with. And this is precisely where the raw coverage advantage concentrated.


Where LeadGenius's raw advantage concentrated


- **Toast** : +27 contacts vs. Clay
- **Upwork** : +27 contacts vs. Clay
- **HubSpot** : +26 contacts vs. Clay
- **Procore** : +25 contacts vs. Clay
- **Zoom** : +25 contacts vs. Clay
- **Uber** : +23 contacts vs. Clay
- **Kaseya** : +22 contacts vs. Clay


It isn't just about finding more names. It's about finding a full buying committee instead of one lonely contact. Across the list, LeadGenius found at least five contacts at 58 accounts; Clay hit that bar at 27, and never found a tenth contact anywhere in the sample.


I don't have employee-count data in this file to prove directly that the gap widens further once you point these same tools at a 40-person company with no press coverage and a marketing ops function that's one person doing five jobs. That's a hypothesis, grounded in how sparse-data problems typically behave, not a finding this spreadsheet can certify on its own. But the direction of the evidence, worse coverage and worse seniority-matching even at the easy end of the market, doesn't point toward the gap closing as the target gets smaller. Smaller companies leave a smaller trail. A provider that's already inferring rather than verifying at this scale has even less signal to work with once the company itself has less signal to give off.


That's the test that actually matters for a team built around the SMB segment: does this gap hold, close, or widen once you run it against the businesses you spend your days chasing. This piece is the appetizer. That's the study that tells you whether the gap is a ceiling or a floor.


Methodology note


Sample: 412 target accounts from a "Top 500 SMB SaaS" vendor list (one duplicate account row excluded from per-account win-rate calculations). Clay was capped at 5 contacts per company at search time; LeadGenius's output is capped to the same 5-contact ceiling here for volume comparisons. Seniority figures reflect each tool's full output before any cap, since seniority and cap are measured independently. Seniority classification uses each provider's own contact-level title, standardized into a common taxonomy (Director/Head, VP, SVP, C-level treated as "Director+"; Manager, Senior Manager, Staff, and unclassified titles treated as below the requested bar). Target titles: GTM engineering, revenue operations, and marketing operations, director level and above.
